newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ bill futures close lower on heavy volume.
newsitem.headline: NZ bill futures close lower on heavy volume.

text.p: Figures in brackets compare against previous day's close
FUTURES PHYSICAL YIELD (PCT)
90-DAY BILLS (JUN) 92.61 (PREV 92.78) 90-DAYS 7.28 (PREV 7.18)
OVERNIGHT CASH 6.70 PCT (PREV 6.70) US 5-YR 6.56 (PREV 6.55)
* NZ short end closes weaker on TWI, MCI concerns
* Eyes on FOMC Wednesday morning NZ time
* Market on alert for potential RBNZ comment
Sharp weakness in the New Zealand bank bill market failed to abate on Tuesday as traders felt concerns about the easiness on monetary policy bite deeper.
There was heavy turnover of 5135 lots in the June bill futures which ended down 17 at 92.61.
The monetary conditions index hovering around 85-90 points in interest rate terms above the Reserve Bank's state desired level made the market extra edgy, dealers said.
A bill dealer said investors were holding off especially while the MCI was close to the Reserve Bank's tolerance level.
"The upside has been vulnerable the last few days and it still feels that way," he said.
Ninety day bills were at 7.28 percent, having started the week at about 7.0 percent.
Traders were hedging their books through the futures and dealers said there was interest to go long on the TWI and short on bill futures in expectation of a Reserve Bank comment soon.
"Tomorrow may be the day when it all happens," the bill dealer said.
"If there is no Fed action we may see the kiwi TWI down with the dollar and then an RB comment later in the morning perhaps. That's the scenario everyone is looking at."
"I don't expect the market to get trashed, but certainly there is scope for a little more weakness yet," said ANZ Investment Bank senior trader Rowan Addison.
But he said he got the feeling the bond market was ready to buy on dips.
Even if the market got a bump from the U.S. after the FOMC decision on Wednesday morning (local time) he said he expected the New Zealand market to outperform.
If the FOMC did not raise U.S. rates, that could lead to dollar weakness and knock-on to a softer Trade-Weighted Index.
Addison said he felt a Reserve Bank comment might not precipitate sustained weakness.

"You have to question what the market will do (if) they come in because I don't think there are too many people around who don't expect (the Bank) to say something. So I expect any weakness on the back of a Reserve Bank comment is going to see some pretty good buying," he said.
-- Simon Louisson, Wellington newsroom, 64 4 4734 746
